name: Fourier's Law of Heat Conduction
statement: Heat flows down a temperature gradient at a rate proportional to its steepness.
meaning: Heat moves spontaneously from hot to cold, and the faster the temperature changes over distance — the steeper the gradient — the faster it flows. A material that conducts well carries more heat for the same gradient. The minus sign in the formula just says the flow runs from high temperature to low.
mechanism: The heat flux equals the thermal conductivity times the negative temperature gradient. Combined with conservation of energy, this yields the heat equation, which governs how temperature spreads through a body over time. Conductivity is an empirical material property, high for metals and low for insulators.

examples.text: Low-conductivity materials like fibreglass and foam cut the heat flow for a given indoor-outdoor temperature difference, slowing heat loss from a building.
High-conductivity metals with large surface area carry heat away from a hot component such as a processor, maximising the flux the law describes.

At the same temperature, metal draws heat from your skin far faster than wood because its conductivity is higher — the sensation is a heat-flux effect, not a temperature difference, exactly what Fourier's law captures.

variants.name: The heat equation
variants.text: The partial differential equation obtained by combining Fourier's law with energy conservation, describing how temperature evolves in space and time.

variants.name: Fick's laws of diffusion
variants.text: The mass-transport analogue, mathematically identical in form — Adolf Fick built his diffusion law by direct analogy to Fourier's heat law.

whyItMatters: It is the founding law of heat conduction, underpinning thermal engineering from insulation and heat sinks to geophysics, and the analogue that inspired the laws of diffusion and the electrical-thermal resistance analogy. The mathematics Fourier invented to solve it — Fourier series — became a pillar of all of physics.

working.text: control heat flow by choosing materials of the right conductivity and by shaping the temperature gradient and area.
treat heat flux like current and temperature difference like voltage to analyse conduction paths as resistance networks.
at nanoscale or ultrafast transients the diffusive law can fail, so use ballistic or hyperbolic models where continuum assumptions break.

limits: It is a phenomenological, empirical constitutive law, not derived from first principles: conductivity is measured, and the law assumes local thermodynamic equilibrium and a continuum. At nanoscale lengths approaching the phonon mean free path, transport becomes ballistic and the diffusive law can fail, though whether this counts as a true breakdown or just needs corrected boundary conditions is debated. Being parabolic, the heat equation also implies an unphysical infinite propagation speed, addressed by hyperbolic Cattaneo-type corrections that impose a finite speed.
misreadings: It is not a fundamental conservation law but a reliable effective description with a measured coefficient and a bounded domain. Its heat equation also does not literally allow instantaneous action at a distance despite predicting it — that infinite speed is an artefact corrected by finite-speed models at short scales.
origin: Set out by the French mathematician Joseph Fourier in Théorie analytique de la chaleur (1822), built on Newton's law of cooling. The same work introduced Fourier series, the technique he devised to solve the heat equation.

sources.text: Thermal conduction, Wikipedia. — the statement, the flux-gradient form, and the heat equation.
